UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )             Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                       )

             MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER OF
                    PPL ELECTRIC UTILITIES CORPORATION

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 PPL Electric Utilities Corporation (“PPL

Electric”) submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer (“Limited Answer”)

to the September 23, 2026 Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the above-captioned proceeding. 2

           PPL Electric reiterates its appreciation for the effort that PJM, its staff, management,

and Board have put into the proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”)

Framework, and submits this Limited Answer solely to highlight an important clarification

regarding the IRAS Filing 3 that PJM provided on page 29 of its September 23 Answer.

Specifically, PJM now clarifies in the record that under its proposal, state regulatory

authorities 4 have the power to ‘opt-out’ individual Eligible New Large Loads from the

requirement to provide IRAS to PJM under the PJM Tariff by granting those Eligible New

    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (Sept. 23, 2026) (“September 23 Answer”).
3
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service & Large Load
Registry, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (Aug. 13, 2026) (“IRAS Filing”).
4
  As used in this filing, “state regulatory authorities” includes Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities
(“RERRAs”), which can include local regulatory authorities.
 Large Loads the ability to “say no” under state law. 5 This fact was not at all clear in PJM’s

initial proposal and implementing tariff language, but if true: (i) raises significant policy

concerns regarding undue discrimination and cost shifting in the application of IRAS across

the PJM Region; and (ii) deepens PPL Electric’s initial concerns regarding the proposal’s legal

foundation under the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).

           PPL Electric respectfully requests that PJM quickly clarify this point in the record, and

that the Commission address it directly in its eventual order, given its importance to the policy

and legal underpinnings of this proceeding.

I.         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

           While an answer to an answer or protest is not a matter of right under the Commission’s

regulations, 6 the Commission routinely permits such answers when the answer provides useful

and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, 7

corrects factual inaccuracies and clarifies the issues, 8 provides information helpful to the




5
  September 23 Answer at 29 (“Third, the IRAS framework does not determine whether any specific retail
customers can say no. Just as the identity of the retail customers who are ultimately implicated by PJM’s directives
to reduce a MW quantity of load is not decided by PJM, under the IRAS framework, it is also not up to PJM to
determine whether, as PPL puts it, retail customers can say no. That—and the regulation of the terms and
conditions of retail rates, and the regulation of retail customers—remains within the exclusive jurisdiction of the
states.”).

                                                         2
 disposition of an issue, 9 or permits the issues to be narrowed. 10 This Limited Answer will

assist the Commission in its decision-making process, clarifies the issues, and provides

information helpful to the disposition of an issue. Accordingly, PPL Electric respectfully

requests that the Commission grant leave and accept this Limited Answer.

II.        LIMITED ANSWER

           In its September 3 Protest, PPL Electric explained that because of how the applicable

tariff language was written, if accepted without modification the IRAS Filing would mark the

first time in history that the Commission would be requiring the mandatory and involuntary

designation of end-use retail customers (Eligible New Large Loads) to provide a FERC-

jurisdictional wholesale rate service (IRAS), and the compulsory provision of that FERC-

jurisdictional wholesale rate service to a Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”)

pursuant to FERC-approved rates, terms, and conditions in a FERC-approved tariff. 11 PPL

Electric explained at length that, while PJM correctly defers to the applicable Electric

Distributor and state regulatory authorities in determining which specific individual Eligible

New Large Loads within a given zone should actually provide IRAS when called upon, the

fact remains that all Eligible New Large Loads (end-use, retail customers) within a zone are

assigned responsibility by PJM to provide this wholesale rate service, pursuant to FERC-

jurisdictional rates, terms, and conditions, and must provide this wholesale rate service to PJM

when called upon. As PPL Electric put it, “[t]he issue is not about which entity gets to identify

the specific individual Eligible New Large Loads that must provide IRAS when PJM calls for



9
    See, e.g., CNG Transmission Corp., 89 FERC ¶ 61,100, at 61,287, n.11 (1999).
10
     See, e.g., New Energy Ventures, Inc. v. S. Cal. Edison Co., 82 FERC ¶ 61,335, at 62,323, n.1 (1998).
11
   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion to Intervene, Protest, and Request for Clarification of PPL Electric
Utilities Corporation at 2 (Sept. 3, 2026) (“September 3 Protest”).



                                                         3
 it,” but rather “[t]he issue is that, when called upon to provide IRAS under that process, the

Eligible New Large Load cannot say no[,] [i]t must, pursuant to a FERC-approved Tariff,

provide IRAS as a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service to PJM.” 12

            In its September 23 Answer, PJM made a critical clarification in response to PPL

Electric’s jurisdictional concerns on page 29:

                   PPL argues, to no avail, that “[t]he issue is not about which
                   entity gets to identify the specific individual Eligible New Large
                   Loads that must provide IRAS when PJM calls for it. The issue
                   is that, when called upon to provide IRAS under that process,
                   the Eligible New Large Load cannot say no.” First, the issue of
                   jurisdiction is about which entity gets to identify the retail
                   customers who ultimately respond to PJM’s directives to reduce
                   load. PJM’s answer is straightforward—the states and/or
                   RERRAs, in coordination with Electric Distributors and their
                   LSEs and retail customers served by those LSEs ultimately
                   identify those retail customers. Second, PJM has, in fact, been
                   continuously consulting and communicating with states and
                   other stakeholders on the design of IRAS for over a year. Third,
                   the IRAS framework does not determine whether any specific
                   retail customers can say no. Just as the identity of the retail
                   customers who are ultimately implicated by PJM’s directives
                   to reduce a MW quantity of load is not decided by PJM, under
                   the IRAS framework, it is also not up to PJM to determine
                   whether, as PPL puts it, retail customers can say no. That—
                   and the regulation of the terms and conditions of retail rates,
                   and the regulation of retail customers—remains within the
                   exclusive jurisdiction of the states. As noted previously, PJM’s
                   load reduction directives will be informed by the degree to
                   which load in a certain zone/area’s IRAS responsibility has been
                   reduced through MW of BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP MW.
                   However, PJM will direct load reduction directives to Electric
                   Distributors, while states/RERRAs may determine which retail
                   customers will implement the load reduction directives.

            The concept that state regulatory authorities have the power to ‘opt-out’ individual

Eligible New Large Loads from the requirement to provide IRAS to PJM under the PJM Tariff



12
     Id. at 10.



                                                   4
 by granting those Eligible New Large Loads the ability to “say no” under retail service terms

and conditions is not at all clear from PJM’s proposed tariff language, but if true is critically

significant.

        Unfortunately, if this is indeed the intent of the IRAS Filing, PPL Electric’s policy and

jurisdictional concerns have only deepened. First, with respect to PPL Electric’s policy

concerns, the implications of PJM’s clarification in its September 23 Answer are striking. If

state regulatory authorities can exempt Eligible New Large Loads from IRAS curtailment

obligations simply by permitting them to “say no” under state law or regulation, then there is

a real risk of disparate treatment and cost shifting in the application of IRAS within the PJM

Region.    Specifically, if Eligible New Large Loads may ‘opt-out’ through localized

arrangements with state regulatory authorities to limit (or even eliminate entirely) their

individual IRAS exposure, the benefits of BYONC in reducing an Eligible New Large Loads’

individual IRAS curtailment exposure are, by definition, undermined. More importantly, the

ability for state regulatory authorities to use that authority to remove the exposure of an Eligible

New Large Load to IRAS curtailment creates the potential for the shifting of cost and reliability

burdens onto other parts of the PJM Region that do not grant such protection. This is a recipe

for undue discrimination in the implementation of IRAS, and constitutes the exact outcome

that PJM is trying to avoid.

        Second, with respect to PPL Electric’s jurisdictional concerns, PJM’s clarification in

its September 23 Answer creates significant ambiguity regarding the legal foundation for IRAS

under the FPA. As PPL Electric noted in its September 3 Protest, IRAS is:

    1. a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service;

    2. established under the FERC-jurisdictional PJM Tariff;




                                                 5
        3. provided by a FERC-defined class of providers (Eligible New Large Loads); and

       4. compensated pursuant to FERC-jurisdictional rates specified in the PJM Tariff.

If the purpose of PJM’s clarification above is to emphasize that, notwithstanding all of these

federal characteristics of IRAS, Eligible New Large Loads are not compelled under federal law

to provide this FERC-jurisdictional wholesale service but instead are only compelled to do so

if the applicable state regulatory authority forces them to, this simply reorients PPL Electric’s

original jurisdictional concern. Specifically, it is unclear under what legal authority state

regulatory authorities in the PJM Region would be able to compel end-use retail customers

(Eligible New Large Loads) to provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service to PJM.

State utility law generally focuses on the entities providing a service to end-use retail

customers, such as distribution utilities, and even then, the service being regulated is one

established under state law itself. To the extent that PJM is imagining that a state would

somehow use its regulatory authority to directly force end-use retail customers to provide this

FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service to PJM, it would be an unprecedented use of state

authority and raise bizarre issues of federalism. This is especially true in light of the fact that

the Commission’s jurisdiction under FPA section 201 is “plenary” and extends “to all

wholesale sales in interstate commerce except those which Congress has made explicitly

subject to regulation by the States.” 13 The FPA does not grant states the ability to compel the

provision of FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate services. To the contrary, “[t]he FPA leaves

no room either for direct state regulation of the prices of interstate wholesales or for regulation

that would indirectly achieve the same result.” 14


13
     F.P.C. v. S. Cal Edison Co., 376 U.S. 205, 216 (1964).
 Fed. Energy Regulatory Comm’n v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 287 (2016) [hereinafter FERC v.
14

EPSA] (citing N. Natural Gas Co. v. State Corp. Comm’n of Kan., 372 U.S. 84, 91 (1963)).



                                                         6
            PPL Electric appreciates the fine line that PJM is attempting to walk under FPA section

201 15 in this proceeding. But given the importance of establishing a sound legal basis for

Commission approval of IRAS, PJM must fully explain and support the actual intent and

jurisdictional basis of its proposal. Put simply:

       1. What legal authority (federal or state/local) is being invoked to force the involuntary
          designation of end-use retail customers to provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate
          service (IRAS), and to compel those end-use retail customers to provide that service to
          PJM at rates, terms, and conditions established under the PJM Tariff?

               a. If the answer is “federal,” then under what provision of the FPA does the
                  Commission have that power?

               b. Alternatively, if the answer is “state,” then again, under what legal basis do state
                  regulatory authorities have this ability, given FERC’s plenary jurisdiction over
                  wholesale rates, services, and markets?

           PPL Electric encourages PJM and the Commission to consider the alternatives that PPL

Electric provided in its September 3 Protest which, if adopted, would strengthen the

jurisdictional foundation upon which IRAS is built. Specifically:


                    Option 1 -

                    Have PJM’s Tariff language stop at the issuance of the
                    Operating Instruction to Electric Distributors to curtail load, and
                    leave the rates, terms, and conditions of that load curtailment
                    service to state and local regulatory authorities—many of whom
                    have already signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. This
                    would avoid a scenario where federally imposed obligations are
                    colliding with state and local-jurisdictional law and tariffs,
                    including the statutory “obligation to serve,” and would provide
                    a much more jurisdictionally sound legal pathway to effectuate
                    connect and manage under FPA section 201.

                    Option 2 -

                    Alternatively, make IRAS a voluntary FERC-jurisdictional
                    service, whereby Electric Distributors and/or large load

15
     16 U.S.C. § 824.



                                                    7
                    customers themselves can voluntarily choose to participate like
                   any other wholesale market service provider in PJM (including
                   demand response providers). Given the enthusiasm with which
                   many large load developers and Electric Distributors have
                   signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, 16 there should clearly
                   be a high level of interest in voluntarily participating in such a
                   program. Such a program would also be consistent with EPSA, 17
                   where the Supreme Court affirmed the Commission’s ability to
                   create programs that “lure,” rather than force, end-use retail
                   customers into participating in FERC-jurisdictional wholesale
                   markets.

III.       CONCLUSION

           In accordance with the foregoing, PPL Electric respectfully requests that the

Commission grant leave and accept this Limited Answer into the record of this proceeding.
